summary:
It's a small resource-management game that places you in a small colony established on Mars, in Gale Crater.

The player must survive as many days as possible by managing the game’s resources as effectively as possible. Surviving sandstorms, cleaning solar panels, timing excursions, drinking water, and eating—all with the goal of reaching the maximum number of days possible while learning to micro-manage their actions more effectively.

Players will gradually learn the long-term consequences of their actions, as well as how to deal with the sudden problems one might face on Mars—such as taking into account Martian cycles, storms, and the cold. All of this will help players develop a strategic mindset with each new game, which will assist them in the future when making decisions in space.
details:
What is My Junior Colonist?


My Junior Colonist is a pixel art survival game where the player is a junior astronaut living in a small base at Gale Crater (4.6°S, 137.4°E), next to NASA’s Curiosity rover. To survive, the player must keep the base powered and warm and manage oxygen, food and water. Outside the base, they also clean dusty solar panels and repair broken ones through a wiring minigame. The twist is that every rule of the game comes from real data:

  • Time: a Martian day (sol) lasts 24 h 39 min 35 s (NASA Mars Facts). The game clock runs on real Martian minutes, sped up ×100.
  • Dust: the TES Dust Cover Index (Mars Global Surveyor), read from NASA Mars Trek for Gale Crater, controls how fast dust builds up on the panels and how often dust storms happen.
  • Energy: the solar panels are based on NASA’s ISS Roll-Out Solar Arrays (iROSA, 20 kW each). Their output is scaled to the sunlight that reaches Mars (586 W/m² vs. 1361 W/m² on Earth, NASA Mars Fact Sheet) and follows the real height of the Sun over Gale Crater, using Mars’ 25.19° axial tilt.
  • Temperature: hour-by-hour air temperatures come from the Mars Climate Database (LMD, with ESA and CNES support). The colder it is outside, the more energy the base needs for heating; if the power runs out, the base slowly cools to the outside temperature.

The game ends when the player runs out of oxygen, stays too long in a base below −10 °C, or goes too long without water (3 sols) or food (14 sols). When you lose, the screen shows how many sols the player survived and their best record, which encourages them to try again and last longer.

Our Impact


Facts about Mars are usually learned as loose numbers that are hard to imagine. Our game turns them into decisions: the player feels that a Martian day is longer, that dust is the biggest threat to solar power (as it was for the Opportunity rover), and that the temperature can change by almost 50 °C in a single sol. We want students and young people to learn how open space data describes another planet, and to understand the real challenges of living on Mars, by playing and understanding their decisions.

What we use?

  • Godot Engine 4.7.2 with C# for the game systems and GDScript for the wiring minigame, as well as GDShaders for the shaders used.
  • NASA Mars Trek, NASA Mars Facts and the NASA Mars Fact Sheet, NASA ISS iROSA data, and the Mars Climate Database web interface, which the game queries over HTTP and caches, with built-in backup data so it also works offline.
  • Pixel art at 16x16, 32x32 and resolution of the window at 320×180, plus GitHub for version control and releases.

Our Minds


Instead of showing data in charts, we incorporated it inside the game rules: a dustier landing site means more frequent storms, the season and latitude change the solar curve, and the outside temperature sets the heating bill. Cartoon-style animations, alerts and minigames keep it fun for a young audience.

What we cared!

  • Scientific accuracy vs. playability: we kept the real relations and ratios, and only scaled what makes a game boring, like the speed of time. We are transparent about it.
  • Accessibility: a simple Windows download that runs without installation.
  • Offline use: the game includes backup data in case it can’t reach the MCD website.
  • Audience: clear goals and short sessions (one sol lasts about 15 real minutes).
  • Credit: every data source is credited to its agency.
